\section{Introduction}
% ============================================================

\begin{frame}{The Judicialization of Electoral Competition}
\hypertarget{src:motivation}{}
\small
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
  \item \textbf{One branch both writes and adjudicates the rules of electoral competition.} The \emph{Justi\c{c}a Eleitoral} settles core terms of the contest by ruling as much as by statute --- councillor seats per municipality, party-loyalty rules, and the gender- and race-fund shares are fixed by TSE and STF decision --- then resolves the disputes those terms generate \ns{\citep{marchetticortez2009,marchetti2012,mozaffar2002}}.\hfill\hyperlink{app:theory}{\beamergotobutton{Theory}}

  \item \textbf{Only the \textcolor{myblue}{adversarial core} matters.} Of the \TotalAllLawsuits{} million filings across the 2020 and 2024 municipal cycles, most is routine administrative paperwork; the disputes fought \emph{between} political actors are the part that bears on who competes and how \ns{\citep{hirschl2008}}.

  \item \textbf{The judiciary's role has widened without the caseload swelling.} New fronts keep opening --- candidate integrity, gender and race inclusion, disinformation, and lately artificial intelligence --- yet adversarial litigation stays roughly flat and \emph{recomposes} across topics rather than rising in volume.\hfill\hyperlink{app:recomp}{\beamergotobutton{Recomposition}}\,\hyperlink{app:timeline}{\beamergotobutton{Timeline}}

  \item \textbf{We study \textcolor{myblue}{intensity}, not a trend.} The object is the adversarial litigation a race faces, identified from \textbf{cross-sectional exposure} rather than an aggregate upward path.
\end{itemize}
\vspace{-2pt}
\begin{block}{Research question}
As a race faces more adversarial litigation, does the contest \textcolor{mygreen}{\emph{level}} (voters re-sort) or does a \textcolor{myred}{\emph{barrier}} emerge (voters withdraw from the ballot) --- and does who runs and who wins change? The vote may concentrate under \emph{either}, so it is the \textbf{ballot} that tells them apart. We ask separately by office; \textbf{the answer differs}.
\end{block}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}[t]{Two Faces of the Same Power: Leveling or Barrier?}
\small
Judicialization can operate through two opposing mechanisms, each running from how the courts are used, through confidence in the process, to how candidates and voters behave. The two make opposite predictions that the data adjudicate.
\vspace{1pt}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
\centering\textbf{\textcolor{mygreen}{\large Leveling}}\\[-1pt]
{\scriptsize accountability $+$ inclusion \ns{\citep{assumpcao2019,ramos2020}}}\\[1pt]
\rule{\linewidth}{0.4pt}\\[1pt]
\raggedright\footnotesize
Courts \textbf{enforce the rules} --- punishing abuse, widening access. The arena is made \emph{fairer}.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
  \item \textbf{Faith} \pos{$\uparrow$} --- the contest reads as legitimate.
  \item \textbf{Candidates} engage; credible challengers not deterred.
  \item \textbf{Voters} express genuine preferences --- more \textbf{valid} votes; they may \emph{re-sort}.
  \item[\ns{?}] \textbf{Competition:} more entrants could \emph{sharpen} it --- or just weed out weak names. \ns{\textbf{Not diagnostic.}}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
\centering\textbf{\textcolor{myred}{\large Barrier}}\\[-1pt]
{\scriptsize litigation as a strategic weapon \ns{\citep{chin2025,nakaguma2025}}}\\[1pt]
\rule{\linewidth}{0.4pt}\\[1pt]
\raggedright\footnotesize
Litigation \textbf{raises the cost} of competing and is wielded by insiders. The arena is made more \emph{forbidding}.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
  \item \textbf{Faith} \negt{$\downarrow$} --- the contest reads as costly or rigged.
  \item \textbf{Candidates} disengage; the entrenched are favoured.
  \item \textbf{Voters} withdraw --- abstain if they can, cast \textbf{null/blank} in discontent; \emph{valid} votes fall.
  \item[\ns{?}] \textbf{Competition:} costs could \emph{concentrate} power --- or felled front-runners could scramble it. \ns{\textbf{Not diagnostic.}}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\vfill
{\footnotesize Two competing hypotheses, tested below --- \pos{\textbf{H1 (Leveling)}}: exposure raises \textbf{valid} voting; \negt{\textbf{H2 (Barrier)}}: exposure raises \textbf{blank} and \textbf{null} voting and lowers valid. They disagree on the \textbf{ballot}, and the ballot is what identifies them --- \emph{not} concentration, which either face can produce.}
\end{frame}


% ------------------------------------------------------------
% --- Timeline moved to Appendix (see \hypertarget{app:timeline}); reached via the Timeline button on the motivation frame. ---


% ------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{This Paper --- Question, Design, Answer}
\footnotesize
The paper asks what happens to the candidate field, to voters, and to the shape of the contest as a race faces more adversarial litigation, and puts an aggregate causal estimate on the answer.
\smallskip

{\setlength{\fboxsep}{6pt}%
\colorbox{mylight}{\parbox{0.96\textwidth}{%
\textbf{\textcolor{myblue}{Design.}} We instrument the $2020\!\to\!2024$ change in adversarial litigation with each municipality's shift-share exposure to national, subject-level litigation diffusion, and read the 2024 outcome net of its clean 2016 baseline (2SLS, state fixed effects, state-clustered standard errors, $N=\NMunis$).}}}
\smallskip

The results fall into four findings, tracing the race from who runs to what it produces, each reported at the confidence it holds:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2pt
  \item \textbf{Candidate supply is unchanged} --- litigation neither thins nor recomposes the field; entry, renewal and descriptive representation are a precise null.
  \item \textbf{Voters withdraw rather than re-sort} --- mayoral blank ($\BlankCoef$) and null ($\NullCoef$) votes rise and valid votes fall, sharpest in contested seats. \ns{Tentative: holds under conventional and exposure-robust inference, not the AR bootstrap.}
  \item \textbf{The mayoral contest concentrates} --- the top-two margin widens ($\MarginCoef$, $p=\MarginP$), the winner's share rises and the runner-up's falls. \ns{Robust: clears the AR wild-cluster bootstrap and the exposure-robust SE.}
  \item \textbf{Who wins does not change} --- the gender and race of the winner do not move.
\end{itemize}
\smallskip
\rule{\linewidth}{0.4pt}\\[3pt]
{\footnotesize These effects are confined to the \emph{mayoral} race. The consolidation is \textbf{general} across seat types; the \textbf{barrier} reading holds where an incumbent is defended --- there, and only there, do voters leave the ballot. The council race exhibits neither face: both the ballot and the composition of the field are flat.}
\end{frame}


% ------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Four Literatures --- and the Gap This Paper Fills}
\footnotesize
Four literatures each name a piece of the phenomenon, but none delivers an aggregate causal estimate of what litigation does to a race. The paper's contribution is located against each in turn.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep4pt
  \item \emph{Judicialization of competition.} A comparative literature documents how courts come to settle the terms of political competition \ns{\citep{tate1995,hirschl2008,sieder2020}}, and in Brazil how the TSE rewrites electoral rules through adjudication \ns{\citep{marchetticortez2009}}. This work is largely descriptive; we estimate the effect on the contest itself.

  \item \emph{Electoral governance.} A second literature studies the fusion of rule-making, application and adjudication within a single branch as a problem of institutional design \ns{\citep{mozaffar2002,marchetti2008,marchetti2012}}. We instead treat litigation intensity as a shock that candidates and voters respond to.

  \item \emph{Lawsuits as strategy versus accountability.} A third body of work reads litigation either as a strategic weapon aimed at rivals \ns{\citep{chin2025,nakaguma2025}} or as a channel through which judicial decisions convey information \ns{\citep{assumpcao2019}}, with campaign money as a driver \ns{\citep{mancuso2023}}. This evidence is case-level and observational; we adjudicate which reading dominates in the aggregate.

  \item \emph{Shift-share identification.} A methodological literature develops topic-based Bartik instruments from leave-one-out flows interacted with pre-period shares \ns{\citep{ash2025,goldsmith2020,borusyak2022,autor2013}}. These designs are built for many diffuse shocks; we adapt the framework to the few, concentrated shocks characteristic of litigation data, relying on the share-exogeneity (GPS) route.
\end{itemize}
\vfill
\centerline{\footnotesize The first three literatures characterise the phenomenon; the fourth allows us to identify it --- an aggregate, causal estimate of litigation's effect on the shape of the contest.}
\end{frame}


% ============================================================
\section{Institutional Background}
% ============================================================

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{The Electoral Justice --- One Branch, Two Roles Over the Contest}
\hypertarget{src:ejustice}{}
\small
A dedicated branch of the judiciary runs and polices Brazilian elections end to end. The \emph{Justi\c{c}a Eleitoral} registers parties and candidates, operates the voting, counts the vote and certifies winners --- and, on the same footing, \textbf{judges the disputes the contest generates}. It is one three-tier hierarchy: the \textbf{TSE} (national), \textbf{27 TREs} (one per state), and $\sim\!\NZonesUniverse{}$ \textbf{zonas eleitorais} presided by ordinary state judges.\hfill\hyperlink{app:geography}{\beamergotobutton{Geography}}
\smallskip

Beyond \emph{administering} the election, two of its powers set the terms of competition --- and they are the object of this paper:
\smallskip
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.49\textwidth}
  \begin{block}{\textcolor{myblue}{Normative} --- it makes the rules}
  \scriptsize Each cycle the TSE issues \emph{resolu\c{c}\~oes} with regulatory force and binding \emph{s\'umulas}; through them (and STF review) it fixes core terms of the contest --- council seats, party loyalty, gender- and race-fund shares, disinformation removal. \hfill\hyperlink{app:timeline}{\beamergotobutton{What it polices}}
  \end{block}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.49\textwidth}
  \begin{block}{\textcolor{myred}{Adjudicative} --- it judges the disputes}
  \scriptsize It resolves the challenges those terms generate, from candidate registration through post-election mandate challenges. Standing is narrow: rivals and the prosecutor sue; \textbf{the voter does not}. \hfill\hyperlink{src:adjudication}{\beamergotobutton{The classes}}
  \end{block}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\smallskip

\footnotesize Created in \textbf{1932} (first \emph{C\'odigo Eleitoral}), dissolved under the 1937 \emph{Estado Novo}, restored in 1945 and constitutionalised in 1946 --- continuous ever since. What has changed is not the branch but the \textbf{reach of these two roles}: the next two frames take each in turn. It is in the \emph{adjudicative} arena that the \textcolor{mygreen}{leveller} and \textcolor{myred}{barrier} faces compete.
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Adjudicative Role --- the Primary Adversarial Classes}
\hypertarget{src:adjudication}{}
\footnotesize
\textbf{The procedural \emph{class} fixes who may sue whom.} Across the adversarial classes the rule is near-uniform: a \emph{candidate}, \emph{party}, \emph{coalition} or the \textbf{Minist\'erio P\'ublico Eleitoral (MPE)} may file against a \textbf{rival candidate} (on majority slates, also the \emph{vice}); the \textbf{ordinary voter has no standing}. The main classes:
\smallskip
\begin{itemize}\itemsep3pt
  \item \textbf{AIRC --- registration challenge} \ns{(LC 64/90)} --- contests a rival's candidacy at registration (ineligibility, \emph{Ficha Limpa}).
  \item \textbf{Representa\c{c}\~ao} \ns{(Lei 9.504)} --- campaign-conduct violations: illicit fundraising, vote-buying (art.~41-A), misuse of office (art.~73).
  \item \textbf{Propaganda / right of reply} \ns{(art.~58)} --- irregular campaign advertising; the offended side answers.
  \item \textbf{AIJE --- judicial investigation} \ns{(LC 64/90 art.~22)} --- abuse of economic or political power.
  \item \textbf{AIME / RCED --- mandate \& diploma challenge} --- post-election action to unseat an elected rival.
  \item \textcolor{mygray}{\textbf{Electoral criminal action} \ns{(MPE-led)} --- the one \emph{vertical}, institution-driven class.}
\end{itemize}
\smallskip
\scriptsize \textbf{Takeaway.} The arena is overwhelmingly \textbf{horizontal --- competitors litigating each other}; the \textbf{MPE is the sole institutional actor} and the \textbf{voter a spectator}. Judicialization here is a \emph{weapon wielded within the political class} --- the litigation-side signature of the ``barrier'' face --- so the instrument tracks the \emph{supply of usable legal weapons across rivals}, not the volume of citizen complaints. \emph{Sources:} Gomes, \emph{Direito Eleitoral} (2024); TSE \emph{Temas Selecionados}.
\end{frame}

\section{Data}
% ============================================================

\begin{frame}{How Does Litigation Affect the Election? Same National Shift, Unequal Local Exposure}
\small
We have described the arena --- an expanding normative reach that hardens into adversarial contests wielded \emph{within} the political class. To estimate its \emph{effect} on a race we need variation in litigation that local politics does not manufacture: municipalities that litigate more are not a random sample of the country.
\smallskip

\textbf{The lever.} National, subject-level litigation trends land \emph{unevenly} across municipalities, according to each one's \emph{prior} caseload mix. Two municipalities meet the \emph{same} national shift with different exposure:
\vspace{2pt}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  font=\footnotesize,
  wave/.style={draw=myblue, thick, rounded corners, fill=myblue!8, align=center, inner sep=5pt},
  muni/.style={draw=black!55, rounded corners, align=center, inner sep=4pt, minimum width=3.3cm},
  hi/.style={-{Latex}, myblue, line width=2.6pt},
  lo/.style={-{Latex}, myblue!45, line width=0.9pt},
]
  \node[wave] (nat) at (0,2.25) {\textbf{National shift} in litigation topic $k$\\ \scriptsize (e.g.\ \emph{fraude \`a cota}) --- measured leave-own-state-out};
  \node[muni, fill=myblue!16] (a) at (-3.5,0) {\textbf{Muni A}\\ \scriptsize \emph{heavy} in $k$ in 2020};
  \node[muni, fill=myblue!4]  (b) at (3.5,0)  {\textbf{Muni B}\\ \scriptsize \emph{light} in $k$ in 2020};
  \draw[hi] (nat) -- (a) node[midway,above left=-2pt]{large push};
  \draw[lo] (nat) -- (b) node[midway,above right=-2pt]{small push};
  \node[below=3pt of a, myblue]   {\scriptsize \textbf{high} predicted exposure $Z_A$};
  \node[below=3pt of b, black!55] {\scriptsize \textbf{low} predicted exposure $Z_B$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\vspace{2pt}
\centerline{\footnotesize \textbf{Same national shift, unequal local exposure} --- we compare municipalities pushed harder by \emph{identical} national trends.}
\smallskip
\footnotesize\textit{What follows builds this lever:} the \textbf{Data} section fixes which filings count and each municipality's 2020 caseload mix; the \textbf{Empirical Strategy} section assembles shares~$\times$~shifts and defends the identifying assumption.
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Adversarial Filter: What Counts as Treatment}
\footnotesize
Most electoral filings are \textbf{mandatory paperwork} --- one candidacy registration (RRC/DRAP) and one finance account (\emph{prestaÃ§Ã£o de contas}) \emph{per candidate}. They move one-for-one with the candidate pool and carry \textbf{no adversarial signal}. Treatment keeps only genuine \textbf{contests between political actors}:
\smallskip

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\resizebox{0.94\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{L{6.0cm}L{6.0cm}}
  \toprule
  \cellcolor{bandvot}\textbf{Kept --- adversarial contests} & \cellcolor{bandlaw}\textbf{Dropped --- administrative / procedural} \\
  \midrule
  Propaganda, disinformation, right of reply & Candidacy registration (RRC / DRAP) \\
  Abuse of economic / political power (AIJE, AIME) & Campaign-finance accounts (\emph{prestaÃ§Ã£o de contas}) \\
  Campaign-finance \& poll-conduct disputes & Vote tallying \& poll-worker admin \\
  Registration \& eligibility \emph{challenges} (\emph{impugnaÃ§Ã£o}, inelegibilidade) & Procedural acts \& enforcement (citation, \emph{cumprimento}) \\
  Originating electoral crimes (vote-buying, \emph{aÃ§Ã£o penal}) & Voter-roll, party-internal, fiscal tail \\
  \bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}
\smallskip

\begin{itemize}\itemsep3pt
  \item \textbf{Routed by subject, gated by class.} A filing is kept on what it is \emph{about}, but its criminal status follows the procedural \emph{vehicle} --- so a registration \emph{challenge} survives even inside the mandatory registration class.
  \item \textbf{What remains:} \KeptAdversarialLawsuits{} adversarial filings, \KeptAdversarialPct\% of the \TotalAllLawsuits{} million total. Treatment $=\Delta\log(1+\ell_m)$, the 2020$\to$2024 change in this count per municipality.
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Recomposition, Not a Wave}
\hypertarget{app:recomp}{}
\footnotesize
The arena does not grow --- it \textbf{rearranges}. Adversarial filings run \textbf{later} (a fatter post-election tail), \textbf{escalate further} (more appeals, higher per-candidate intensity), and tilt toward \textbf{gender-quota fraud}, while the broad topic mix barely moves.
\smallskip
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.50\linewidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.44\textheight,keepaspectratio]{../figures/litigation_timing_shape.pdf}\\[4pt]
{\scriptsize\ns{Filings by week relative to the vote, each cycle normalised to its own total. Both peak in the final fortnight; 2024 (blue) carries the fatter post-vote tail.}}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.48\linewidth}
\centering
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/litigation_composition.tex}}\\[4pt]
{\scriptsize\ns{Topic shares (top) barely move; the \textbf{character} rows (bottom) do --- filings run later, appeal more, and per-candidate escalation rises by half.}}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\smallskip
{\centering\scriptsize \textbf{Why it matters for identification:} this is a \emph{national} recomposition, and it reaches each municipality through its \emph{own} 2020 topic mix --- the same shift, unequal local exposure. That is the lever the instrument exploits.\par}
\smallskip

% ============================================================
\section{Empirical Strategy}
% ============================================================
\subsection{What We Estimate}

\begin{frame}{What We're Measuring: Level the Field, or Raise the Bar?}
\small
We do not ask who wins a \emph{given} seat, but whether heavier \textbf{candidate-vs-candidate} litigation reshapes the \emph{contest itself}. Three layers, each measured as a \textbf{2020\,$\to$\,2024 change}; the \emph{sign} of the effect tells the two faces apart.
\vspace{10pt}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.7}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l l c c@{}}
\toprule
 & \textbf{What we measure} & \textcolor{mygreen}{\textbf{Leveller widens}} & \textcolor{myred}{\textbf{Barrier narrows}} \\
\midrule
\textbf{1\ \ Who runs} & Entrants, women \& non-white candidates, party count, field size & broader pool & fewer, safer names \\
\textbf{2\ \ How voters respond} & Turnout, blank \& null votes & voters stay engaged & voters drop off \\
\textbf{3\ \ How open it stays} & Victory margin, effective \# of candidates, incumbency advantage & \emph{ambiguous} & consolidation \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}
\vspace{10pt}
{\centering\footnotesize Together these are the two behavioral engines --- \textbf{candidates} and \textbf{voters} --- and the \textbf{result} they produce, the spine of the Results section. Layer 2 is the \textbf{discriminating} layer: layer 3 concentrates under either face, so the ballot assigns one. Next, the equation, then the instrument behind it.\par}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{The Specification: Instrument Litigation, Condition on the 2016 Baseline}
\hypertarget{src:spec}{}
\small
\textbf{First stage (OLS)} --- instrument the change in litigation intensity:
\[
\underbrace{\Delta\log(1+\ell_{m})}_{\text{endogenous}} \;=\; \alpha + \beta\, \bZ + \mathbf{X}_m'\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \delta_{\text{UF}(m)} + \varepsilon_m
\]
\textbf{Second stage (2SLS) --- ANCOVA on the 2016 pre-window baseline:}
\[
Y_{m,2024} \;=\; \alpha + \tau\, \widehat{\Delta\log(1+\ell_{m})} + \lambda\, Y_{m,2016} + \mathbf{X}_m'\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \delta_{\text{UF}(m)} + u_m
\]
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
  \item $\ell_m$ = adversarial lawsuits (originating filings in the cycle) resolved to the municipality of origin; $\Delta$ = first difference 2024$-$2020.
  \item \textbf{Outcome in levels, on a clean 2016 baseline.} $Y_{m,2016}$ predates the 2020 exposure shares (a true pre-treatment lag); $\lambda$ is \emph{freely estimated} and $\tau$ reads the 2024 level holding 2016 fixed.
  \item \hypertarget{src:fd}{}\textbf{Why ANCOVA, not first differences.} Municipal outcomes barely persist, so first differences (which pin $\lambda=1$) over-difference and attenuate --- FD is an appendix check \hyperlink{app:fd}{\beamergotobutton{FD bracket}}; outcomes with no clean 2016 analog stay in FD.
  \item $\mathbf{X}_m$ = 6 pre-determined controls (log population, urbanisation, log income p.c., 2010 higher-education share, 2020 valid-vote volume, 2016 victory margin); $\delta_{\text{UF}(m)}$ = state FE (\NClusters{} of 27 UFs). SE clustered by state.
\end{itemize}
\centerline{\footnotesize \hyperlink{app:readtau}{\beamergotobutton{How to read the coefficient $\tau$}}}
\end{frame}


\subsection{The Instrument}

\begin{frame}{Constructing the Instrument: Shares $\times$ Shifts}
\footnotesize
The instrument combines a \textbf{pre-determined 2020 exposure share} with a \textbf{leave-own-state-out national shift}, at the \textbf{subject} level (\NSubjectsKept{} kept TSE subjects --- no family aggregation is imposed on $\bZ$).
\smallskip

\textbf{Shares} --- each municipality's 2020 adversarial-subject mix, fixed two cycles before 2024 outcomes:
\[
s_{m,k,2020} \;=\; \frac{\text{adversarial lawsuits of subject } k \text{ in } m,\ 2020}{\text{all adversarial lawsuits in } m,\ 2020},
\qquad \sum_k s_{m,k,2020}=1.
\]
\textbf{Shifts} --- each subject's log caseload growth, summed over \emph{all other states}:
\[
g_{\text{UF}(m),\,k} \;=\; \log\!\bigl(1 + L_{-\text{UF},\,k,\,2024}\bigr) - \log\!\bigl(1 + L_{-\text{UF},\,k,\,2020}\bigr),
\qquad L_{-\text{UF},\,k,\,t} = L^{\text{nat}}_{k,t} - L^{\text{own-UF}}_{k,t}.
\]
\textbf{Instrument} --- the portfolio-weighted predicted exposure, one number per municipality:
\[
\bZ \;=\; \sum_{k} \; \underbrace{s_{m,k,2020}}_{\text{share (pre-determined)}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{g_{\text{UF}(m),\,k}}_{\text{shift (other states)}}
\]
\smallskip
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2pt
  \item \textbf{Leave-own-state-out} purges any local litigation wave: a municipality's shift excludes its whole state, so every municipality in a state shares the same per-subject shift and state FE absorb it --- identification comes from \textbf{within-state variation in the 2020 shares} (the zone\,$\subset$\,state adjudication locus is set out earlier, in the Research Design section).
  \item Variation is off subjects that diffuse \textbf{across states} --- jurisprudence, MPE priorities, party legal strategy --- not local politics. The same $\bZ$ is carried into the executive and legislative designs.
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{The Instrument Across Brazil}
\footnotesize
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}
  \centering

\end{column}

\begin{frame}{The First Stage: Strong, Linear, and Stable}
\hypertarget{src:firststage}{}
\footnotesize
Constructed exposure moves \emph{realized} litigation: regressing the 2020$\to$2024 change in adversarial filings on $\bZ$ (controls $+$ state FE) gives a precise positive coefficient, cluster-robust effective $F=\HeadlineF$ --- far above the weak-instrument threshold. Inference uses the $tF$ correction \citep{lee2022}.
\smallskip

\end{column}

The fix corrects two stale claims: (i) the mayoral blank rate straddles zero (p=ARBlankP=0.108), it does NOT exclude zero; (ii) the exposure-robust bound inflates the margin SE by only ERMarginRatio=1.06x, so the consolidation DOES clear it.

\subsection{Identification \& Inference}

\begin{frame}{Identification \& Inference, in Brief}
\hypertarget{src:identbrief}{}
\small
The instrument is \textbf{share-identified}: with only $K_{\text{eff}}=\KeffRotemberg$ effective shocks, credibility rests on the \textbf{exogeneity of the 2020 caseload shares}, not on averaging many independent shifters \citep{goldsmith2020,borusyak2022}. Three checks carry it, each with a full appendix.
\medskip
\begin{itemize}\itemsep4pt
  \item \textbf{What does the identifying work.} A handful of national \emph{propaganda}-regulation shocks carry most of the Rotemberg weight --- concentrated, but \emph{not} weak (own $F_k$ well above conventional thresholds). \hfill\hyperlink{app:rotemberg}{\beamergotobutton{Rotemberg weights}}
  \item \textbf{The shares carry the \emph{adversarial} signal.} Conditioning on non-adversarial filing intensity leaves the estimate unmoved, and a placebo Bartik built from the \emph{excluded} mandatory filings is null. \hfill\hyperlink{app:shares}{\beamergotobutton{Defending the shares}}
  \item \textbf{Inference is weak-IV- and few-cluster-robust.} State clustering leaves \NClusters{} clusters, so headline $p$-values come from an Anderson--Rubin wild-cluster bootstrap; a BHJ/AKM exposure-robust bound barely moves the margin SE. \hfill\hyperlink{app:inference}{\beamergotobutton{Inference}}
\end{itemize}
\smallskip
\takeaway{\textbf{How to read every result that follows.} One estimator throughout: \textbf{2SLS} of the outcome on instrumented $\Delta\log(1+\text{adversarial lawsuits})$, each outcome the \textbf{2024 value on its 2016 baseline} (ANCOVA), \textbf{state FE}, \textbf{state-clustered} SEs. In every coefficient plot the \textbf{thick} bar is the 90\% CI, the \textbf{thin} bar the weak-IV $tF$ 95\% CI, and \textcolor{myred}{\textbf{red}} marks a point distinguishable from zero. Strip magnitudes are per \textbf{one-SD rise in judicialization} ($\approx\TreatSDMult\times$ litigation). Not repeated below.}
\end{frame}

% finding (ANCOVA-2016, AR-WCR-confirmed), against precise nulls on

\section{Results}

\begin{frame}{The Story in One Frame --- Two Engines, One Result}
\small
An election is produced by two behaviours: \textbf{candidates} decide whether to run and how to campaign; \textbf{voters} decide whether to turn out and how to mark the ballot. We isolate the contest's \textbf{judicial dimension} --- adversarial decisions and the presence / noise of litigation --- and ask how each engine responds and what they jointly produce.
\vspace{-4pt}
\begin{center}
\scalebox{0.97}{
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  font=\scriptsize,
  exp/.style={draw=myblue, thick, rounded corners, fill=myblue!8, align=center, inner sep=5pt, text width=8.6cm},
  eng/.style={draw, rounded corners, align=center, inner sep=5pt, minimum height=1.75cm, text width=3.6cm},
  res/.style={draw, rounded corners, align=center, inner sep=5pt, minimum height=1.4cm, text width=6.4cm},
  flow/.style={-{Latex}, myblue, line width=1.4pt},
]
  \node[exp] (exp) at (0,2.25)
    {\textbf{The contest's judicial dimension}\\[1pt]adversarial decisions $+$ the presence / noise of litigation \;(exposure measured by the instrument)};
  \node[eng, fill=mygray!8] (cand) at (-2.9,0.4)
    {\textcolor{myblue}{\textbf{Candidates}}\\[1pt]\ns{who runs \& how they campaign}\\[1pt]
     \colorbox{mygray!30}{\textbf{\,null\,}}\\[1pt]
     {field \& funding unmoved}};
  \node[eng, fill=myred!6] (vot) at (2.9,0.4)
    {\textcolor{myblue}{\textbf{Voters}}\\[1pt]\ns{turnout \& the ballot}\\[1pt]
     \colorbox{myred!20}{\textcolor{myred}{\textbf{\,withdraw\,}}}\\[1pt]
     {blanks \& nulls rise, valid falls}};
  \node[res, fill=myred!6] (res) at (0,-1.55)
    {\textcolor{myblue}{\textbf{The election result}} \;\ns{concentration \& who is elected}\\[1pt]
     \colorbox{myred!20}{\textcolor{myred}{\textbf{\,consolidates\,}}}\;\colorbox{mygray!30}{\textbf{\,who wins: null\,}}\\[1pt]
     {top-two margin widens ($\MarginCoef$); winner's identity unchanged}};
  \draw[flow] (exp) -- (cand);
  \draw[flow] (exp) -- (vot);
  \draw[flow] (cand) -- (res);
  \draw[flow] (vot) -- (res);
\end{tikzpicture}
}
\end{center}
\vspace{-4pt}
\footnotesize The candidate engine is quiet while voters withdraw \emph{where an incumbent is defended}; the consolidation --- general across seats --- is the electorate re-allocating toward the leader, not candidates removed. Concentration alone does not name a face: the \textbf{barrier} reading rests on the ballot, and so holds for \textbf{contested} seats. The council race is null throughout.
\end{frame}


% ============================================================
\subsection{The Result --- What the Contest Produces}
% ============================================================

\begin{frame}{The Mayoral Race Consolidates: the Top-Two Margin Widens}
\hypertarget{src:spine1}{}
\small
The winner's vote share rises, the runner-up's falls, and the top-two margin between them widens --- all three point one way: toward \textbf{consolidation}, not a candidate-removing \pos{weapon}. This is the headline result; the frames that follow ask who it favours, decompose which engine produced it, and show where it lands.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/executive_iv_competition.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\takeaway{A one-SD rise in judicialization widens the winner's margin by $+\MarginPerSD$~pp ($p=\MarginP$), lifts the winner's share by $+\WinSharePerSD$~pp, and cuts the runner-up's by $\RunnerUpPerSDSigned$~pp. Margin and runner-up both clear the weak-IV-robust AR bootstrap (margin $\ARMarginCI$, $p=\ARMarginP$) --- the finding that carries statistical weight.}
\smallskip
\scriptsize\ns{Whole-field concentration points the same way but is individually imprecise \hyperlink{app:concentration}{\beamergotobutton{whole-field}}; discretisations appendixed \hyperlink{app:compbinary}{\beamergotobutton{closeness}}.}\hfill\hyperlink{app:multiplicity}{\beamergotobutton{multiple testing \& index}}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Who the Consolidation Favours: the Incumbent, Not a Demographic}
\hypertarget{src:favored}{}
\small
Consolidation reinforces whoever is already ahead --- so who \emph{is} that? Profiling the 2024 mayoral field by within-race vote rank answers it descriptively, before any regression: the winner and the runner-up part on \textbf{political standing}, not demographics. The front-runner is a sitting incumbent roughly five times as often; on gender, race, education, and age the top-two are near-twins.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{!}{0.23\textheight}{\input{../tables/tex/candidate_rank_profile.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\takeaway{Because the top-two are demographically interchangeable, widening the margin between them entrenches \textbf{incumbency} --- a neutral trait --- which is mechanically why the vote-weighted gender / race composition (next frame) cannot move. What is protected is incumbency, not a sex or a colour. \ns{Descriptive shares by vote rank; no causal content.}}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Litigation Does Not Reshape Who Wins the Mayoral Race}
\hypertarget{src:representation}{}
\small
If consolidation moved the margin but not the identities, the vote-weighted composition of winners should be flat --- and it is. The vote-weighted gender, race, and incumbency mix, and the winner's own identity, are a precise null: the margin moves, the person does not. This is the one place \emph{cassa\c{c}\~ao} could move the winning name (entrant typology \hyperlink{src:entrant}{\beamergotobutton{here}}).
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.46\textheight,keepaspectratio]{../figures/representation_coefplot.pdf}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\takeaway{Every interval straddles zero: a one-SD shock moves the female vote share by $\FemaleVSPerSDSigned$~pp and the probability the winner is female by $\FemaleWinPerSDSigned$~pp, neither distinguishable from zero. Litigation neither advances nor suppresses descriptive representation on net.}\hfill\hyperlink{app:representation}{\beamergotobutton{Full table}}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Whose Share Moves? The Gender Incidence of the Consolidation}
\hypertarget{src:gender}{}
\small
``On net'' can hide an offsetting transfer, so we open the consolidation itself. It moves vote from the runner-up's slot to the winner's; splitting \emph{both} slots by the office-seeker's gender asks who pays and who collects. The split is \textbf{unconditional} --- the components sum back exactly to the totals on the previous frames, same $N$, nothing conditioned on who placed where \hyperlink{app:gender}{\beamergotobutton{construct \& full tables}}.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.32\textheight,keepaspectratio]{../figures/gender_consolidation_coefplot.pdf}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\takeaway{\textbf{The cost is gender-neutral; the gain may not be.} The runner-up's loss splits evenly (female $\FemRUSharePerSDSigned$~pp, male $\MaleRUSharePerSDSigned$~pp) and that slot's gap is a \emph{precisely estimated} zero ($\RUGapCoef$, $p=\RUGapP$) --- not merely inconclusive. The gain lands on \textbf{male} front-runners ($\MaleWinSharePerSDSigned$~pp, $p=\MaleWinShareP$) while the female winner's share is flat ($p=\FemWinShareP$), but that slot's differential test is $\WinGapPerSDSigned$~pp, $p=\WinGapP$: \negt{suggestive, not established}. Net, women's share of the top two drifts down $\FemTopTwoPerSDSigned$~pp ($p=\FemTopTwoP$).}
\smallskip
\scriptsize\ns{The incidence the previous two frames predict: if the top-two are demographic near-twins \hyperlink{src:favored}{\beamergotobutton{who it favours}}, widening the margin between them should be gender-blind on the losing side --- and it is. Exploratory, outside the declared family, raw $p$ \hyperlink{app:multiplicity}{\beamergotobutton{multiplicity}}.}
\end{frame}


% ============================================================
\subsection{Which Engine Moved? --- Candidates vs Voters}
% ============================================================

\begin{frame}{Engine 1 --- Candidates: Who Runs Does Not Move, in Either Office}
\hypertarget{src:candidates}{}
\small
Litigation could thin the field as a \negt{barrier} (it is costly to mount and defend, and \emph{cassa\c{c}\~ao} can annul a candidacy) or open it as a \pos{weapon} (challengers and courts can remove front-runners) --- so the sign is \emph{a priori} ambiguous. Entry is an anticipation margin: candidacies register at the August deadline, before most suits resolve. It resolves to neither force --- across both offices, and across field size, gender, race, education, entry, and incumbency, every candidate-supply margin is a null.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.44\textheight,keepaspectratio]{../figures/candidate_supply_coefplot.pdf}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\takeaway{No supply margin moves in either office: mayoral field size ($\CandExecCoef$, $p=\CandExecP$), its female ($\FemaleCandCoef$, $p=\FemaleCandP$), non-white, higher-ed, new-entrant and incumbent shares, and the council pool ($\LegCandCoef$, $p=\LegCandP$) all straddle zero. Mean age is flat in the mayoral field (\MayorAgeYr~yr); the council pool skews marginally younger (\CouncilAgeYr~yr, $p=\CouncilAgeP$) --- a lone wrinkle that fails multiple testing. Whatever reshapes the race is the other engine, the \textbf{voters}.}\hfill\hyperlink{app:compbinary}{\beamergotobutton{count table}}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Engine 2 --- Litigation Pushes Voters Off the Mayoral Ballot}
\hypertarget{src:voterballot}{}
\small
Turnout is \textbf{compulsory} in Brazil (ages 18--69), so it is institutionally floored --- but a voter can still decline to choose, casting a \textbf{blank} or \textbf{null} ballot that elects no one. With turnout pinned, demobilisation shows up as a rise in these non-valid votes and a fall in valid ones. That is the mayoral pattern below; the pooled council ballot stays flat.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{!}{0.22\textheight}{\input{../tables/tex/executive_iv_ballot_mayoral.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\takeaway{A one-SD shock raises the mayoral blank rate by $+\BlankPerSD$~pp and the null rate by $+\NullPerSD$~pp, cutting valid votes by $\ValidPerSDSigned$~pp. The blank rise clears conventional and exposure-robust SEs ($p=\BlankP$; $\ERBlankPbhj$) but not the weak-IV AR bootstrap ($p=\ARBlankP$) --- the more tentative of the two live findings. It concentrates in \emph{contested} mayoral seats, not open ones (next frame). The pooled \emph{council} ballot, by contrast, stays flat.}\hfill\hyperlink{app:turnoutplacebo}{\beamergotobutton{turnout placebo}}\,\hyperlink{app:councilplacebo}{\beamergotobutton{council placebo}}
\end{frame}


% ============================================================
\subsection{Heterogeneity --- Two Channels by Seat Type}
% ============================================================

\begin{frame}{The Identifying Test --- Which Face, by Seat Type}
\hypertarget{src:seathet}{}
\small
Split the mayoral races by whether the seat is \textbf{open} --- the incumbent is term-limited, so no front-runner defends it ($N=2{,}026$) --- or \textbf{contested}, where the sitting mayor may still seek re-election ($N=3{,}534$). This split is what \emph{assigns} the face: the vote concentrates in both, so only the ballot separates them.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.44\textheight,keepaspectratio]{../figures/heterogeneity_seat_coefplot.pdf}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\takeaway{The winner's top-two margin widens in \emph{both} seat types ($+0.076$, $p=.05$ open; $+0.068$, $p=.01$ contested) --- consolidation is general. The \emph{mechanism} splits by seat: in \textbf{open} seats it is \pos{decisiveness}, the winner crossing 50\% ($+0.160$, $p=.06$) with no ballot demobilisation. In \textbf{contested} seats it is a \negt{barrier} signature --- blank votes rise ($+0.005$, $p=.04$) and valid votes fall ($-0.013$, $p=.08$) as voters confront an entrenched incumbent, with no majority shift ($p=.74$). One shock: decisiveness where the seat is open, disengagement where it is defended.}\hfill\hyperlink{app:seathet}{\beamergotobutton{full table}}
\end{frame}


% ============================================================
\section{Robustness}
% ============================================================

\begin{frame}{The Robustness Program --- Four Threats, Four Verdicts}
\footnotesize
The design rests on a few concentrated shocks and an extensive-margin first stage, so credibility comes from a battery of checks, not a large-sample law of large numbers.
\smallskip
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.05}
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{2.7cm} p{5.9cm} c @{\hskip 5pt}p{2.1cm}@{}}
\toprule\toprule
\textbf{Threat} & \textbf{Check} & \textbf{Verdict} & \textbf{Appendix} \\
\midrule
Is the identifying variation what we claim? &
Reduced form survives dropping every zero-litigation municipality and a presence dummy; count-native Poisson/NegBin confirm the weak intensive margin is a \emph{real} null. Read it as the \emph{onset} of contestation. &
\tick &
\hyperlink{app:extensive}{\beamergotobutton{extensive}}\, \hyperlink{app:reclass}{\beamergotobutton{reclass}} \\
\midrule
Does the treatment definition drive it? &
Invariant across log1p, IHS, level, rate, and binary definitions; only weak-first-stage transforms lose significance --- a weak-IV symptom, not counter-evidence. &
\tick &
\hyperlink{app:tdef}{\beamergotobutton{treat.\ def.}} \\
\midrule
Is the inference honest? &
Consolidation clears the weak-IV-robust AR bootstrap and the BHJ/AKM exposure-robust SE (the outer bound; CI still excludes zero). First differences are a conservative bracket. &
\tick &
\hyperlink{app:exposure}{\beamergotobutton{weak-IV}}\, \hyperlink{app:fd}{\beamergotobutton{FD}} \\
\midrule
Is it multiple testing? &
Survives a Romano--Wolf correction and loads onto a barrier/closeness index, with no favourable family cut; pre-trend placebos are clean throughout. &
\tick &
\hyperlink{app:multiplicity}{\beamergotobutton{mult.}}\, \hyperlink{app:pretrend}{\beamergotobutton{pre-trend}} \\
\bottomrule\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize The consolidation clears every threat; the disengagement stays tentative (clears exposure-robust, not the AR bootstrap); the nulls stay null.
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Consolidation Measures Are Pre-Trend Clean}
\hypertarget{src:pretrend}{}
\small
A free 2016 lag raises a fair question: does the instrument load on municipalities already moving in the consolidating direction? To test this we regress the 2016$\to$2020 pre-period change on the instrument, conditioning only on pre-determined (2010 Census) covariates and state FE. A clean, share-exogenous design wants every coefficient near zero, since the shock should not predict past movement.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.44\textheight,keepaspectratio]{../figures/pretrend_coefplot.pdf}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize Every consolidation measure is clean --- margin ($p=\PtMarginP$), effective-N ($p=\PtEffNP$), Herfindahl ($p=\PtHHIP$), top-two share ($p=\PtTopTwoP$) all straddle zero, as does ballot composition. One honest caveat: turnout pre-trends ($p<.01$) --- the convergence the first stage rides --- and the valid share, an electorate share, mechanically inherits it; consolidation and ballot composition are untouched. Adding the 2020 level as a second lag moves nothing \hyperlink{app:ptrobust}{\beamergotobutton{full pre-path}}. \emph{(Thick 90\%, thin 95\% CI; red $p<.05$.)}\hfill\hyperlink{app:pretrend}{\beamergotobutton{Placebo table}}
\end{frame}

% ============================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% ============================================================

\begin{frame}{What the Design Shows --- Findings by Confidence}
\hypertarget{src:findings}{}
\footnotesize
On the clean 2016 baseline the evidence sorts into three tiers of confidence:
\medskip
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
  \item[\textcolor{myred}{\rule{1.2ex}{1.2ex}}] \textbf{Robust --- the mayoral race consolidates.} The top-two margin widens ($\MarginCoef$, $p=\MarginP$), the winner's share rises ($\WinShareCoef$) and the runner-up's falls ($\RunnerUpCoef$). It clears the weak-IV-robust AR wild-cluster bootstrap (margin $p=\ARMarginP$, runner-up $p=\ARRunnerUpP$), the BHJ/AKM exposure-robust SE (CI $\ERMarginCI$ excludes zero), and multiplicity correction at 5\% by Holm and Benjamini--Hochberg (Romano--Wolf, the most conservative of the three, clears at 10\%: $p=.059$) --- the finding that carries statistical weight.
  \item[\textcolor{myred!55}{\rule{1.2ex}{1.2ex}}] \textbf{Tentative --- voters disengage on the same ballot.} Mayoral blank ($\BlankCoef$) and null ($\NullCoef$) votes rise and valid votes fall, concentrated in contested seats, while compulsory turnout stays pinned. Significant under conventional and exposure-robust inference (exposure-robust $p=\ERBlankPbhj$) but not the AR bootstrap ($p=\ARBlankP$).
  \item[\textcolor{mygray}{\rule{1.2ex}{1.2ex}}] \textbf{Precise nulls.} Descriptive representation and renewal, the entrant typology, elastic and education-stratified turnout, campaign finance, and the entire legislative side --- all tightly bounded around zero. The consolidation's \emph{cost} belongs here too: the runner-up's loss splits evenly by gender ($\RUGapCoef$, $p=\RUGapP$) \hyperlink{src:gender}{\beamergotobutton{gender}}.
  \item[\textcolor{mygray!55}{\rule{1.2ex}{1.2ex}}] \textbf{Exploratory --- who collects the gain.} The winner's gain lands on male front-runners ($\MaleWinSharePerSDSigned$~pp, $p=\MaleWinShareP$) with the female winner's share flat, but the differential test does not clear ($p=\WinGapP$) and these outcomes sit outside the declared family. A direction the data suggest and do not establish.
\end{itemize}
\medskip
\footnotesize The candidate engine is quiet while some voters withdraw, so the consolidation is the electorate re-allocating votes toward the leader, not candidates removed. Note the structure of the claim: the \textbf{consolidation is robust}, while the \textbf{barrier reading is tentative} --- it rests on the ballot, one tier down.\hfill\hyperlink{app:abstract}{\beamergotobutton{summary table}}\, \hyperlink{src:mechanism}{\beamergotobutton{mechanism}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Contribution}
\small
Where a large literature reads courts as a \pos{leveller} that opens contests to under-represented entrants, the evidence here documents the opposite margin: in single-winner municipal races, an expanded judicial arena \textbf{re-concentrates} the vote toward the front-runner without reshaping who runs or who wins --- and, where an incumbent is defended, pushes marginal voters off the ballot, the \negt{barrier} signature.
\medskip

The shift-share design isolates this from the nation-wide litigation trends common to every race, and the sharp \textbf{mayoral-versus-council asymmetry} shows the mechanism is specific to the single-winner contest rather than a general effect of legal activity.
\medskip

The reframing matters as much as the sign. The relevant margin of judicialization is its \emph{expanded role} --- rule-making, weaponization, and the anticipation of both --- of which observed lawsuit counts are only the visible tip. The barrier operates even as raw filings hold flat or fall.
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Limitations}
\small
Three bound the reach of the claim.
\medskip
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep6pt
  \item \textbf{Few effective shocks.} Identification rests on $K_{\text{eff}}=\KeffRotemberg$ effective shocks --- \RotPropagandaPct\% of the weight on propaganda subjects --- and \NClusters{} clusters, so a many-shock law of large numbers does not apply; the design is defended on the exogeneity of the 2020 shares (balance and pre-trend), not on shock count.
  \item \textbf{Extensive-margin identification.} The first stage moves the treatment on the extensive margin, so the per-unit-of-volume magnitude is not well identified even though the existence and sign of the effect are; the estimate is a local effect for onset compliers.
  \item \textbf{Aggregate, not case-level.} The treatment is municipal-level litigation intensity, not any single suit, so the design speaks to the aggregate climate of judicialization a race faces, not to the outcome of a specific case.
\end{enumerate}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Theoretical Framework: Signal vs Weapon}
\hypertarget{app:theory}{}
\footnotesize
The \textbf{Leveling} and \textbf{Barrier} faces of the main text rest on two hypotheses about \emph{why} litigation moves an election:
\smallskip
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.49\textwidth}
  \begin{block}{H1 --- Accountability / signal}
  \scriptsize Courts sanction abuse; a filing reveals candidate type $\Rightarrow$ cleaner competitors advance. \hfill\ns{\citep{assumpcao2019}}
  \end{block}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.49\textwidth}
  \begin{block}{H2 --- Weaponization / noise}
  \scriptsize Litigation as campaign weapon: aimed up the ladder, judicially weak, media-amplified $\Rightarrow$ sways voters, not judges. \hfill\ns{\citep{chin2025,nakaguma2025}}
  \end{block}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\smallskip

\textbf{Why the testable split is Leveling vs.\ Barrier, not H1 vs.\ H2.} Voters cannot tell a genuine charge from a strategic one, so an accountability signal (H1) and a \emph{sticky} weapon (an H2 that changes minds) look alike --- \textbf{both move votes toward someone}, the \textbf{Leveling} signature. What the data \emph{can} separate is whether litigation moves votes at all (Leveling) or merely \textbf{fouls the contest without re-sorting} (Barrier). The three mechanisms collapse onto one observable axis:
\smallskip
\begin{center}\scriptsize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
\textbf{Mechanism} & \textbf{Observable face}\\
\midrule
H1 accountability signal & \textbf{Leveling} --- cleaner types advance; votes re-sort\\
H2 weapon that \emph{sticks} (persuades) & \textbf{Leveling} --- votes move; indistinguishable from H1\\
H2 weapon that only \emph{fouls} & \textbf{Barrier} --- blank/null $\uparrow$, valid $\downarrow$; no re-sorting\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\centerline{The design identifies \textbf{Leveling vs.\ Barrier} (frame 3); it does \emph{not} separate H1 from a sticky H2. \hfill\hyperlink{src:motivation}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back}}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- How to Read the Coefficient $\tau$}
\hypertarget{app:readtau}{}
\small
The headline number in every table is $\tau$, the 2SLS coefficient on the \emph{instrumented} change in litigation. Three things fix its meaning:
\smallskip
\begin{itemize}\itemsep3pt
  \item \textbf{Treatment is a log-change.} $\Delta\log(1+\ell_m)$ is (approximately) the \emph{proportional} growth in a municipality's adversarial caseload, $2020\to2024$. A one-unit rise is litigation multiplied by $e$ ($\approx+170\%$); a \textbf{doubling} of lawsuits is a $\log 2 \approx 0.69$ rise. So $\tau$ is the outcome change ``per unit of log-growth in litigation,'' and $0.69\,\tau$ is the change per doubling.
  \item \textbf{Outcome is a 2024 level, net of its 2016 baseline.} Because the outcome is a 2024 level conditioned on its 2016 baseline, $\tau$ is the effect on \emph{where a municipality ends up in 2024}, holding its 2016 starting point fixed --- not on a change score. Shares, rates, and margins are in $[0,1]$, so $\tau=0.092$ means $+9.2$ \textbf{percentage points} (compare to the ``Mean of dep.\ var.'' row).
  \item \textbf{It is a LATE for onset compliers.} 2SLS recovers the effect for municipalities whose litigation actually responds to the diffusing national shock --- not an average over all \NMunis. The first stage is identified off the \emph{extensive} margin (whether a contest enters the judicial arena at all; see \hyperlink{app:extensive}{extensive-margin appendix}), so the compliers are municipalities crossing \emph{into} adversarial contestation, not those scaling up an existing caseload.
\end{itemize}
\smallskip
\footnotesize \textbf{Worked example (top-two margin, $\tau=\MarginCoef$).} A municipality whose adversarial litigation \emph{doubled} relative to another ends 2024 with a margin $0.69\times\MarginCoef\approx\MarginDoublePP$ percentage points wider, starting from the same 2016 margin --- against a 2024 mean of \MarginMean. Equivalently, a one-unit rise in predicted exposure (the Bartik index) raises litigation growth by $\FSCoef$ of a log-unit (first stage), i.e.\ a $\approx\MarginRFperUnitPP$pp wider margin in reduced form.\hfill\hyperlink{src:spec}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to spec}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Identification: Pure First-Difference Bracket}
\hypertarget{app:fd}{}
\small
The headline conditions the 2024 level on the 2016 baseline ($Y_{2024}\sim D + Y_{2016}$, $\lambda$ freely estimated). This appendix re-estimates the \emph{same} headline outcomes as a pure first difference ($\Delta Y \sim D$), which pins the persistence coefficient $\lambda=1$.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/appendix_first_difference.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize \textbf{Over-differencing attenuates.} Municipal margins barely persist from one cross-section to the next, so forcing $\lambda=1$ over-differences: the consolidation and disengagement coefficients collapse toward zero and lose significance. The contrast is the point --- freeing $\lambda$ is the appropriate estimator for a barely-persistent outcome, not a specification that manufactures the result. Dep.\ var.\ means are $\Delta$ means; state (UF) FE; SEs clustered by state. \hfill\hyperlink{src:fd}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to spec}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- What Identifies It: Few Concentrated Shocks (Rotemberg)}
\hypertarget{app:rotemberg}{}
\footnotesize
\textbf{\textcolor{myblue}{A Goldsmith--Pinkham (GPS) share-identified design, not a many-shock LLN.}} With only $K_{\text{eff}}=\KeffRotemberg$ effective shocks, credibility rests on the \emph{exogeneity of the 2020 shares}, not on averaging away many independent shifters \citep{goldsmith2020,borusyak2022}. The Rotemberg decomposition assigns each subject a weight $\alpha_k$ (summing to one) measuring how much it drives the 2SLS estimate --- and the weight is concentrated on a handful.
\smallskip
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.55\textwidth}
\centering\scriptsize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Highest-weight subject} & $\alpha_k$ (\%) & Own $F_k$ \\
\midrule
\RotNameOne   & \RotPctOne   & \RotFOne \\
\RotNameTwo   & \RotPctTwo   & \RotFTwo \\
\RotNameThree & \RotPctThree & \RotFThree \\
\RotNameFour  & \RotPctFour  & \RotFFour \\
\RotNameFive  & \RotPctFive  & \RotFFive \\
\midrule
\textit{Top five} & \textbf{\RotTopFiveCumPct} & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\\[3pt]
{\tiny All five are \emph{Propaganda Eleitoral} subjects.}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.43\textwidth}
\scriptsize
\textbf{The estimate is propaganda-diffusion.} The five highest-weight subjects carry \RotTopFiveCumPct\% of the net weight, and propaganda subjects carry \textbf{\RotPropagandaPct\%} of it (this Rotemberg weight measures leverage on the \emph{estimate}, so it runs above propaganda's \RecPropShare\% share of the instrument's raw variation). They are \emph{not} weak (own $F_k$ of \RotFOne, \RotFTwo, \ldots), so the concentration is not a weak-instrument artifact --- a few national propaganda-regulation shocks (internet rules, timing, permitted media) do the identifying work.
\medskip

\textbf{Not a contradiction with propaganda \emph{falling}.} Propaganda litigation declines nationally, but identification does not use that trend --- it uses \textbf{leave-own-state-out variation in each topic's growth \emph{across} states}, so a topic can shrink on average yet still diffuse unevenly enough to identify. The exclusion restriction must then hold \emph{for propaganda specifically}: the share-exogeneity checks (next) test that the 2020 shares carry the adversarial signal rather than pre-trends or generic litigiousness; the distinct worry --- that a \emph{national} propaganda recode or a direct regulatory channel drives the shift --- is taken up separately \hyperlink{app:reclass}{\beamergotobutton{coding artifact?}}.
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\smallskip
\footnotesize The concentration is \textbf{intrinsic to litigation data}, not a modelling choice: a finer partition raises the shock count but destroys first-stage relevance. So we defend the design on the \textbf{exogeneity of the shares} --- balance, pre-trend, and a placebo shifter (next frame) --- not on a shock-count law of large numbers.
\smallskip
\centerline{\hyperlink{src:identbrief}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back}}}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Defending the Shares: Non-Adversarial Intensity and a Placebo Shifter}
\hypertarget{app:shares}{}
\footnotesize
The exogenous-shares path requires that the 2020 exposure shares isolate the \emph{adversarial} channel rather than proxy a municipality's overall litigiousness. Two checks (full BHJ treatment):
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
  \item \textbf{Intensity control.} Add the 2020 \emph{level} of non-adversarial (mandatory/administrative) filings as a pre-determined control. If the shares proxied generic litigation volume, conditioning on it would move the estimate. It does not (margin $\PlaceboMainCoef\!\to\!\PlaceboIntensCoef$).
  \item \textbf{Placebo shifter.} Build an identically-constructed Bartik from the \emph{excluded} mandatory/administrative filings. Its reduced form is null (margin $\PlaceboRFCoef$, SE $\PlaceboRFSE$) and it has near-zero own relevance ($F=\PlaceboRelevanceF$) --- it does not predict litigation growth, as a non-channel should not.
\end{itemize}
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{!}{0.30\textheight}{\input{../tables/tex/nonadversarial_robustness.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize \emph{Columns:} main IV; $+$ non-adversarial intensity; $+$ placebo Bartik control; placebo reduced form. The main coefficient is unmoved by conditioning on either, and the placebo channel is null throughout --- the shares carry the adversarial signal, not generic litigiousness.
\smallskip
\centerline{\hyperlink{src:identbrief}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back}}}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Inference: Few Clusters and the Exposure-Robust Bound}
\hypertarget{app:inference}{}
\footnotesize
The point estimate is invariant to how we compute standard errors; only precision --- and the weak-IV verdict --- moves. We cluster at the \textbf{state} level, where the leave-own-state shift is constant.
\smallskip
\begin{itemize}\itemsep3pt
  \item \textbf{Why state.} With a shift-share instrument, residuals correlate across units sharing shocks \citep{adao2019}; here the shifter is identical within a state, so state clustering is the principled, conservative default.
  \item \textbf{Few clusters $\Rightarrow$ weak-IV-robust AR.} State clustering leaves only \textbf{\NClusters{} clusters}, where asymptotic cluster-robust SEs can under-cover. Headline inference is therefore carried by an Anderson--Rubin \textbf{wild-cluster restricted bootstrap} ($B=9999$, Rademacher weights over \ARNClusters{} states). It \emph{confirms} the consolidation --- margin $p=\ARMarginP$, runner-up share $p=\ARRunnerUpP$, both excluding zero --- while the mayoral \textbf{blank rate stays tentative} (AR set straddles zero, $p=\ARBlankP$) and the null outcomes (turnout, winner-majority, female share) stay null.
  \item \textbf{Exposure-robust outer bound.} The BHJ/AKM standard error --- built for the few-shock shift-share structure, re-clustering at the subject (shock) level --- inflates the headline margin SE by only $\ERMarginRatio\times$, so \textbf{the consolidation still clears}; the SE barely moves because the estimate does not hang on one dominant shock. \hfill\hyperlink{app:exposure}{\beamergotobutton{weak-IV \& exposure-robust appendix}}
\end{itemize}

\centerline{\hyperlink{src:identbrief}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back}}}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Weak-IV and Exposure-Robust Inference}
\hypertarget{app:exposure}{}
\small
The headline uses conventional state-clustered standard errors. Two stress tests bracket that choice --- one for weak instruments, one for the few-shock shift-share structure.
\smallskip

\textbf{(a) Anderson--Rubin wild-cluster restricted bootstrap} (\ARNClusters{} state clusters) --- weak-IV-robust: it inverts the AR statistic and is valid regardless of instrument strength.
\begin{center}\scriptsize\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Outcome & AR 95\% CI & $p$ \\
\midrule
Top-two margin        & \ARMarginCI   & \ARMarginP \\
Runner-up vote share  & \ARRunnerUpCI & \ARRunnerUpP \\
Mayoral blank rate    & \ARBlankCI    & \ARBlankP \\
Turnout (placebo)     & \ARTurnoutCI  & \ARTurnoutP \\
Female vote share     & \ARFemaleVSCI & \ARFemaleVSP \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\scriptsize The consolidation (margin, runner-up) clears; the disengagement (blank) CI straddles zero --- the tentative finding; the compulsory-turnout placebo and the representation null are (correctly) indistinguishable from zero.
\smallskip

\textbf{(b) BHJ/AKM exposure-robust standard error} --- the honest outer bound for a design identified off a handful of diffusing litigation topics; it re-clusters at the shock (subject) level.
\begin{center}\footnotesize
Top-two margin: conventional SE $\ERMarginSEconv \to$ exposure-robust $\ERMarginSEbhj$ (a $\ERMarginRatio\times$ inflation); $p=\ERMarginPbhj$; null-imposed CI $\ERMarginCI$ excludes zero.
\end{center}
\footnotesize Even under the most conservative shock-level clustering the consolidation survives --- the SE barely moves because the estimate does not hang on a single dominant shock. \hfill\hyperlink{src:spine1}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to the margin}}
\end{frame}

% RELEVANCE is extensive (intensive slope F=1.1) and confirms it is NOT a log1p
% artifact via count-native Poisson/NegBin (both null intensive); Panel B shows
% the OUTCOME is not extensive (margin RF survives dropping zeros + a horse race
% vs the presence dummy). Then reframed: the extensive margin IS the meaningful

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Is the Identification Just Zero-vs-Any Litigation?}
\hypertarget{app:extensive}{}
\footnotesize
\noindent \textbf{The concern.} \ExtMassPointPct\% of municipalities (\ExtMassPointN{}) have \emph{zero} adversarial litigation in the 2020 base year --- a mass point at the origin of $\Delta\log(1+\ell_m)$. So a fair reader asks whether the first stage, and the finding, merely ride the crude \textbf{zero-vs-any} switch rather than the shift-share \emph{composition} the construction advertises.
\smallskip
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.53\linewidth}
\centering
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/extensive_margin.tex}}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.45\linewidth}
{\scriptsize
\textbf{Panel A --- relevance \emph{is} mostly extensive, and we say so.} Among litigating municipalities only the intensive slope collapses ($F=\ExtFSintensiveF$); the presence dummy alone is mechanically hyper-predictive (its \emph{negative} sign is the log1p floor --- a zero-litigation muni can only grow --- the \textbf{convergence} the first stage identifies off).\par
\textbf{Not a log1p artifact.} A count model has no floor, yet returns the \emph{same} verdict: modelling the caseload natively (Poisson / NegBin ANCOVA, zeros absorbed directly) leaves $Z$ with no proportional effect conditional on the 2020 baseline (PPML $p=\ExtPPMLfullP$, NegBin $p=\ExtNBfullP$; null among litigators too) --- the weak intensive margin is \emph{real}.\par
\textbf{Panel B --- the finding is \emph{not} extensive.} The margin reduced form survives (i) dropping the entire zero mass point (litigating-only $p=\ExtRFpositiveP$) and (ii) a horse race vs.\ the presence dummy --- $Z$ stays significant ($p=\ExtRFhorseZP$), presence wrong-signed and null ($p=\ExtRFhorseDzeroP$). Only \ExtZonDzeroRtwo{} of $Z$'s variance is presence.\par}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
{\centering\scriptsize \textbf{Read --- a feature, not a flaw.} $Z$ predicts \emph{whether} a contest enters the judicial arena, not the caseload once in --- but that \textbf{onset of adversarial contestation} \emph{is} the expanded-role treatment. The outcome response is not a zero-vs-any jump (Panel B), so 2SLS is a clean LATE for these \emph{onset compliers}; only the per-unit-\emph{volume} magnitude leans on the extensive first stage.\par}
\smallskip
\centerline{\hyperlink{src:firststage}{\beamerreturnbutton{First stage}}\quad\hyperlink{app:tdef}{\beamergotobutton{Does the log1p form drive it?}}\quad\hyperlink{src:spine1}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to the margin}}}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Companion to app:extensive: is the finding an artifact of the log1p treatment
% definition? Re-estimates the headline margin 2SLS under 5 ways of measuring the
% litigation change, SAME Bartik Z. The teaching point: the reduced form (margin~Z)
% is ONE number invariant to the treatment transform, so only the units and the
% first-stage F move. Numbers from treatment_definition{,_macros}.tex (12_...R).
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Does the log1p Treatment Definition Drive the Result?}
\hypertarget{app:tdef}{}
\footnotesize
\noindent The endogenous variable is $\Delta\log(1+\ell)$. The $\log(1+\cdot)$ form is a modelling choice --- it compresses large counts and floors at zero. A fair reader asks whether the consolidation survives \emph{other} reasonable ways to measure the change in litigation. We re-estimate the headline ANCOVA-2016 margin 2SLS under \TdefNdefs{} treatment definitions, holding the \emph{same} Bartik instrument, controls, state FE, and clustering fixed.
\smallskip
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.54\linewidth}
\centering
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/treatment_definition.tex}}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.44\linewidth}
{\scriptsize
\textbf{The finding never changes sign; the units do.} The single fact organising the table: the \emph{reduced form} $\text{margin}\sim Z$ is \textbf{one number} ($\TdefRFcoef$, $p=\TdefRFp$), \emph{invariant} to how the treatment is transformed. Each 2SLS column is just that fixed reduced form divided by a definition-specific first stage --- so only the magnitude units and the first-stage $F$ move.\par
\smallskip
The instrument predicts the \emph{compressed} treatments strongly (log1p, IHS, onset: $F$ up to \TdefFhi) and the \emph{raw-count} magnitude weakly (levels, rate: $F$ as low as \TdefFlo). So where significance softens it is a \textbf{weak-instrument} symptom of the raw-count first stage, not counter-evidence --- the same extensive-margin fact as the previous slide. The per-1-SD effect stays positive throughout.\par}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\smallskip
{\centering\scriptsize \textbf{Read.} Existence, sign, and significance of the consolidation are robust to the treatment definition; the per-\emph{unit} magnitude is definition-dependent (Chen--Roth 2023) --- which is exactly why the reduced form, not a units-laden 2SLS coefficient, is the honest headline object.\par}
\smallskip
\centerline{\hyperlink{app:extensive}{\beamerreturnbutton{Extensive margin}}\quad\hyperlink{app:reclass}{\beamergotobutton{Is the shifter a coding artifact?}}\quad\hyperlink{src:spine1}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to the margin}}}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Confronts topic-reclassification of the SHIFTER (assunto codes changing between
% 2020 and 2024). Honest, partly-uncomfortable frame: the instrument is 71%
% propaganda national shift (negative). Family-level Z (immune to within-family
% recode) keeps F=177, margin RF p=0.079; dropping propaganda entirely collapses
% the first stage (F=2.0) -- so identification rests on the propaganda decline being
% BEHAVIOURAL (regime substitution: litigation -> takedowns), which is the thesis.
% Numbers from reclassification_robustness{,_macros}.tex (13_...R).
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Is the Shifter a Topic-Reclassification Artifact?}
\hypertarget{app:reclass}{}
\footnotesize
\noindent The shifts are leave-own-state-out national growth rates of each \emph{assunto} (subject) code. If TSE recoded a case type between 2020 and 2024, a subject's national growth is spurious --- and leave-own-state-out does \emph{not} absorb it, because a \emph{national} recode hits every state at once. The exposure is concrete: \RecPropShare\% of the instrument's variation is the \textbf{propaganda} national shift, and that shift is \emph{negative} ($\RecPropShock$) --- propaganda is precisely the topic with documented recoding and regime substitution.
\smallskip
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.55\linewidth}
\centering
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/reclassification_robustness.tex}}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.43\linewidth}
{\scriptsize
\textbf{The unit is the \emph{subject}, not the vehicle.} The shifter is built on the \emph{assunto} (what the case is \emph{about}), not the \emph{classe} (procedural vehicle) --- so the documented propaganda$\leftrightarrow$Representa\c{c}\~ao recode, a \emph{vehicle} relabeling, does not move the shifter's units.\par
\smallskip
\textbf{Within-family recode is not it either.} Rebuilding the instrument at the topic-\emph{family} level makes it \emph{immune} to reclassification that reshuffles cases among subjects inside a family: the first stage stays strong ($F=\RecFamF$) and the margin reduced form stays positive ($\RecFamRFcoef$), though it \emph{softens} to $p=\RecFamRFp$ --- corroborating, not decisive.\par
\smallskip
\textbf{The honest limit.} Dropping propaganda's shift \emph{entirely} collapses the first stage ($F=\RecNoPropF$): the instrument \emph{is} the propaganda decline. So identification rests on that decline being \textbf{behavioural, not a coding artifact} --- and it is: the 2020--2024 fall in propaganda \emph{litigation} is the documented substitution of case-by-case suits by administrative and platform \textbf{takedown orders}. That shift in the arena's \emph{mode} is the paper's ``expanded, partly-unmeasured role'' --- not a relabeling.\par}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\smallskip
{\centering\scriptsize \textbf{Read.} The result survives within-family reclassification (family $F=\RecFamF$, RF softening to $p=\RecFamRFp$); it is \emph{not} separable from the propaganda national shift, which we defend substantively as a real change in how the judiciary polices campaigns rather than a dictionary change.\par}
\smallskip
\centerline{\hyperlink{app:tdef}{\beamerreturnbutton{Treatment definition}}\quad\hyperlink{src:firststage}{\beamerreturnbutton{First stage}}\quad\hyperlink{src:spine1}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to the margin}}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Many Outcomes, No Family Cut}
\hypertarget{app:multiplicity}{}
\footnotesize
The barrier reading rests on a family of correlated outcomes, so a fair reader asks: does it survive multiple-testing correction? We answer \emph{without} having to declare which outcomes ``count'' --- two complementary routes that both sidestep that arbitrary choice.
\smallskip

\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.52\linewidth}
\scriptsize \textbf{(a) Collapse each theory-declared family to one index} (Anderson 2008 inverse-covariance / Kling--Liebman--Katz standardized average). One family $=$ one test $=$ no within-family multiplicity. Each 2024 index is taken net of its own 2016 baseline; effects are in standard-deviation units, oriented so positive $=$ consolidation/barrier.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/summary_indices.tex}}
\end{center}
\scriptsize The \textbf{overall barrier index clears} ($p<.05$) and closeness clears on its own; the representation and council-ballot placebo indices are null. The pattern holds with \emph{no} confirmatory-family choice.
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.46\linewidth}
\scriptsize \textbf{(b) Romano--Wolf stepdown} over all 18 barrier/representation reduced forms --- a \emph{joint} wild-cluster bootstrap ($B=10{,}000$, shared Rademacher weights) controlling the family-wise error rate.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/romano_wolf_stepdown.tex}}
\end{center}
\scriptsize Margin and runner-up survive raw and Holm; at the fully simultaneous family-wise \emph{plus} few-cluster level they land borderline ($p_{\text{RW}}\!\approx\!.06$) --- honest, not damning: RW is stricter than normal-approx Holm because the bootstrap captures the \ARNClusters{}-cluster tails the index averages over.
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\smallskip
\footnotesize \textbf{Read.} The \emph{finding is the pattern}, not a single star: the index --- which needs no family cut --- clears; the most-corrected single coefficient is borderline, which is what \ARNClusters{} clusters buy. \ns{The family is fixed at these 18 and was not re-opened afterwards: the gender decomposition \hyperlink{src:gender}{\beamergotobutton{gender}} is an exploratory split of an outcome already inside it, reported at raw $p$ and never counted as a new confirmatory test.} \hfill\hyperlink{src:spine1}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to the margin}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Pre-Trend Placebo (consolidation ladder, numeric)}
\hypertarget{app:pretrend}{}
\small
The numeric placebo behind the balance coefplot: the \textbf{2016$\to$2020} pre-period change in each consolidation outcome, regressed on the (instrumented) 2020$\to$2024 treatment --- a future shock cannot cause a past change, so a clean design wants $\approx 0$. Conditioned on \emph{pre-determined} (2010 Census) covariates only; state FE; state-clustered.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/pretrend_falsification.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize \textbf{Every rung clean} --- margin ($\PtMarginCoef$, $p=\PtMarginP$), effective-N ($\PtEffNCoef$, $p=\PtEffNP$), Herfindahl ($\PtHHICoef$, $p=\PtHHIP$), top-two share ($\PtTopTwoCoef$, $p=\PtTopTwoP$). \textbf{Why this differs from an earlier draft:} conditioning the balance test on \texttt{margin\_2016} --- the ladder's own 2016 baseline --- induced a regression-to-the-mean (Lord's-paradox) artifact that read as a pre-trend; dropping it (the baseline is inadmissible when the outcome is a 2016-based change) clears every rung. \hfill\hyperlink{src:pretrend}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to balance test}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Consolidation Robust to the Full Pre-Treatment Path}
\hypertarget{app:ptrobust}{}
\small
\textbf{Even the stricter test leaves it unchanged.} The balance test already clears the consolidation measures; as a further check we \emph{add} the \textbf{2020 base-year level} to the headline 2016 lag, so the two lags $\{2016, 2020\}$ span both \emph{where} a municipality started and the \emph{pre-slope} it was on. The 2020 level is pre-determined w.r.t.\ the 2020$\to$2024 shock (the instrument's shares are dated 2020, the shifter leaves the state out), so it is a legitimate control --- the coefficient is now identified off the 2024 deviation \emph{from each municipality's own path}.
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/executive_iv_concentration_ptrobust.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize \textbf{Essentially unchanged.} The top-two margin barely moves from its headline value ($\MarginCoef$) and stays significant at 5\%; effective-N and the Herfindahl shift only in the third decimal and remain imprecise, exactly as in the headline. Conditioning on both the 2020 level and the pre-slope a municipality was on moves nothing: the consolidation is a response to the 2020$\to$2024 shock, not the continuation of a pre-existing path. \hfill\hyperlink{src:pretrend}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to balance test}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Whole-Field Concentration Measures}
\hypertarget{app:concentration}{}
\small
Beyond the top-two gap, three measures read concentration across the \emph{whole} field: the effective number of candidates (Laakso--Taagepera), the vote-share Herfindahl, and the combined top-two share. Same headline spec (2024 level on the 2016 baseline, state FE, clustered by state).
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/executive_iv_concentration.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize The Herfindahl rises ($\HHICoef$, $p=\HHIP$, sig.\ at 10\%) and effective-N moves the consolidating way ($\EffNCoef$) but imprecisely ($p=\EffNP$); the combined top-two share is flat ($\TopTwoCoef$, $p=\TopTwoP$). They agree in direction --- the redistribution is \emph{within} the leading pair, runner-up to winner, not two parties crowding out the rest --- but the top-two margin carries the statistical weight, so these corroborate rather than confirm. \hfill\hyperlink{src:spine1}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to the margin}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Candidates (Mayoral): Closeness Robustness (binary / raw count)}
\hypertarget{app:compbinary}{}
\small
Two closeness outcomes kept off the main top-two margin table. The \textbf{winner-majority} indicator (did the winner clear 50\% of valid votes) is the underpowered binary discretisation of the continuous margin; the \textbf{log candidate count} is the raw-count analog of the effective number of candidates already in the concentration measures. Same baseline spec (2024 value on 2016 level, state FE, state-clustered).
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{0.6\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/appendix_competition_binary.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize \textbf{Same direction, weaker instruments of measurement.} Both carry the consolidation sign --- winner-majority positive, log-count negative (fewer candidates) --- but the binary indicator is too noisy to clear significance on its own, and the raw count is only marginal; the continuous top-two margin and the effective-N count are the better-powered forms. \hfill\hyperlink{src:spine1}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back to the margin}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Appendix --- Campaign-Spending Attrition: the Direct Candidate Channel}
\hypertarget{app:spending}{}
\hypertarget{src:mechanism}{}
\small
Does litigation drain a challenger's war chest faster than the front-runner's, tilting the contest before a vote is cast? A 2SLS of judicialization on the 2020$\to$2024 change in TSE campaign spending (SPCE contracted expenses; 99.8\% of ranked mayoral candidates matched), cut by vote rank --- front-runner (1st) vs challenger (2nd) --- and by seat type. Attrition predicts the challenger's spend, and their share of the top-two, falling under exposure, sharpest where an incumbent is defended. Baseline controls; state FE; state-clustered; first stage $F=62$--$102$ (precise nulls, not weak-IV).
\smallskip
\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../tables/tex/mechanism_finance_seat.tex}}
\end{center}
\smallskip
\footnotesize Attrition is suggestive, not proven. On the full sample every spending outcome is null; in contested seats the signs line up (challenger's spend falls, front-runner's holds, challenger's top-two share slips) but are far from significant (best $p\approx.22$). So the measured candidate channel is \emph{not} the money --- it is voter disengagement in these same contested seats \hyperlink{src:voterballot}{\beamergotobutton{disengagement}}: soft challenger support blanks out rather than being out-financed. \hfill\hyperlink{app:seatdisengage}{\beamerreturnbutton{Back}}
\end{frame}
